short: An interview that asks every candidate the same job-related questions in the same order and scores each answer on the same anchored scale; the most valid single predictor in the 2022 re-estimation.
A conversational interview without fixed questions or a scoring scale; it predicts job performance at .19 in the 2022 re-estimation and dilutes stronger evidence when added to it.
The validity a meta-analysis reports for a selection method against job performance after its corrections; the 2022 re-estimation revised the main figures downward by .10 to .20.
The narrowing of score variance when only screened or incumbent people are studied; how far to correct for it is the dispute behind the 2022 revision of selection validity.
Validity evidence showing that scores on a selection procedure relate to measures of job performance; one of the three strategies the Uniform Guidelines accept.
A test of general mental ability; moved from the focal predictor (.51) to a mid-table one (.31) in the 2022 re-estimation, and the predictor with the largest Black–White difference (d .79).
A test in which candidates perform a sample of the actual work, scored against a standard; validity .33 in the 2022 re-estimation with a Black–White d of .67.
A test of the knowledge a job requires; second to the structured interview in the 2022 re-estimation at .40, with a Black–White d of .54.
Scored biographical information about a candidate; empirically keyed biodata predicts at .38 in the 2022 re-estimation and is among the procedures applicants like least.
A selection test the 2022 re-estimation lists as SJT (knowledge) at an operational validity of .26, with a Black–White d of .39; no lever in the pack rests on it.
A test of honesty or integrity; .31 validity with one of the smallest Black–White differences (d .10) in the 2022 re-estimation, and one of the procedures applicants like least.
A selection method listed in the 2022 re-estimation at .29 operational validity with a Black–White d of .52, down from .37 in the 1998 baseline.
A test of traits such as conscientiousness; conscientiousness predicts at .19 in the 2022 re-estimation with a negligible group difference, and applicants rate personality tests low.
How applicants perceive a selection procedure; perceptions predict attraction, offer acceptance and withdrawal, and interviews and work samples are the best liked.
Telling candidates the hard parts of the job and the firm before they decide; across 40 studies previews lowered inflated expectations and turnover, mainly by signaling honesty.
Combining predictor scores by formula and treating the total as the anchor for the decision; it predicts job performance at r .44 against .28 for judgment.
Combining selection evidence holistically, by judgment or feel instead of by formula; it costs more than a third of the achievable validity (r .28 against .44).
The standardized gap (d) between group means on a predictor; cognitive ability tests show the largest Black–White d (.79) and structured interviews one of the smallest (.23).
A substantially lower rate of selection for a race, sex or ethnic group; under the Uniform Guidelines a rate below four-fifths of the highest group's is generally regarded as evidence of it.
The Uniform Guidelines' rule of thumb: a group's selection rate below four-fifths (eighty percent) of the highest group's is generally regarded as evidence of adverse impact.
The 1978 framework (29 CFR 1607) the EEOC, DOL, DOJ and the Civil Service Commission adopted for judging selection procedures under Title VII: records by group, the four-fifths test, validation.
A study showing that a selection procedure relates to job performance; predictive studies follow applicants, concurrent studies test incumbents, and the two need different corrections.
The study of a job from which selection criteria, interview competencies and work samples are derived; the Uniform Guidelines tie validity to important elements of job performance.
A requirement the job actually needs, as distinct from a preference inherited from the customer or an incumbent; the guide asks that each be labeled contractual, customer-required or preferred.
The live-coding or whiteboard interview used for software roles; in a randomized trial being watched halved performance on the same problem and raised measured stress.
Days from requisition opening to accepted offer; the 2025 SHRM median is about 45 days for executive and nonexecutive roles alike.
A recruiting metric the pack carries no definition or benchmark for; the measure the pack's records carry is time to fill, a 2025 median of about 45 days.
Candidates who stop responding during the process or after accepting; 41 percent of organizations reported it rising in 2025.
An accepted hire who never starts; 4.1 percent of 157,154 accepted offers at one employer, with each week between acceptance and start raising the odds by about a fifth.
Offers accepted over offers extended; in the one field study earlier post-interview offers were more often accepted, with no later performance or turnover penalty.
A published pooling of many studies' effect sizes; the guide's highest evidence grade, quoted with its k and N as reported.
The size of a relationship or difference as a study reports it (a correlation, a d, an odds ratio, a percentage); the guide quotes each exactly, with its population and statistic.
A measure of how closely two quantities move together, written r when observed and ρ when corrected; the guide's validity figures and turnover predictors are correlations.
The ratio of the odds of an outcome between two conditions; 1.22 per extra week of offer-to-start interval means each week raised the odds of a no-show by about a fifth.
k is the number of studies and N the total sample behind a meta-analytic estimate; the guide quotes both with every effect size, as reported.
A randomized or natural experiment in real hiring or employment settings; the guide's second evidence grade.
Difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity or matched designs on administrative or firm data; the guide's third evidence grade.
A quasi-experimental design that compares states that adopted a law with states that did not, before and after; the guide's pay-transparency and salary-history evidence uses it.
A survey of HR professionals or employers by an association or vendor; carried for benchmark facts only, with publisher and year named, never as evidence of a lever's effect.
The label on every lever, constraint and link saying what kind of evidence stands behind it, from meta-analysis down to synthesis; defined on the methods page.
The guide's label for a conclusion no cited work states on its own; the lowest evidence grade, marked visibly wherever it appears.
The record of the author's original staffing matrix, every row and category carried as a hypothesis and adjudicated against the evidence; never a source of fact.
One of the eight observed failure points in patterns.yaml, written as a recruiter sees it; the pathfinder's first question, pointing at the constraints that explain it.
A record of something that binds an opening at one stage: what it is, why it happens, how to tell, which levers and gates apply, who decides, and its evidence grade.
A record of something the firm can do about a constraint, with its evidence grade, the effect exactly as reported, what it does not do, its costs and the constraints it can worsen.
A record of a regulatory or contractual rule that binds an opening regardless of evidence, with its governing text, thresholds, steps and pending changes.
A record of a public data source, program, reference, standard or tooling category a recruiter can put to work, recorded as its owner states it; no vendor is recommended.
A record of a headline figure with its reference period, publication date, publisher and series; never timeless, shown in the node panels of the constraints that cite it.
An edge in links.yaml between two records, with a relation (precondition, amplifies, trade-off, enables), a short label and its own cited evidence; the graph draws exactly these.
The app's deterministic narrowing page: failure pattern, stage, role conditions and state, scored and ranked, never recommended, then passed to the graph as the highlighted set.
The browser-local notepad for one opening: pinned constraints, chosen levers, owner, decision date and measure; exported as Markdown or JSON, never leaving the browser.
A computational tool that makes or supports an employment decision; New York City, California and Colorado define and regulate it under different names (AEDT, ADS, ADMT).
Using software, an algorithm or AI to screen, rank, score or interview candidates; a selection procedure under the Uniform Guidelines, with state notice, audit and retention duties on top.
A neutral selection procedure that disproportionately excludes a protected group; lawful only if job-related and consistent with business necessity, and open to a less discriminatory alternative.
A question asked of applicants before a conditional offer; the ADA, the Fair Chance Act, the citizenship-status rule and the salary-history bans each reserve or restrict particular questions.
The federal Fair Chance to Compete for Jobs Act: since December 20, 2021 a contractor may not ask about criminal history for positions under a federal contract until after a conditional offer.
State and local fair-chance laws that take the criminal-history question off the application or delay it to an interview or a conditional offer; fifteen states cover private employers.
A contract-defined class of labor under a time-and-materials or labor-hour contract, with its own fixed hourly rate and its own qualifications.
The education and experience line a contract attaches to a labor category; only labor that meets it can be billed at the category rate.
A contract type that pays fixed hourly rates per labor category, under a ceiling price, for work whose extent or duration could not be estimated at award.
The multiplier that turns a salary into a billing rate by loading fringe, overhead, G&A and profit; the pack marks the arithmetic as synthesis.
The first layer of a billing rate: fringe benefit cost expressed as a rate on direct labor.
The second layer of a billing rate: indirect cost applied to direct labor plus fringe.
The G&A layer of a billing rate: general and administrative expense applied to total cost input, after fringe and overhead.
The profit element of a billing rate, entered as a rate on top of fringe, overhead and G&A; the pack's offer records call it fee.
The government audit agency the rate build-up names as an approver of a contractor's indirect rates.
The OFPP benchmark above which compensation is unallowable on covered contracts: $671,000 for 2025 by an accounting firm's figure.
A cost the government will reimburse or recognize in rates under the FAR Part 31 cost principles; an unallowable cost stays with the firm.
The FAR cost principle on compensation for personal services: reasonableness, an established plan, the bonus rule and the compensation cap.
The federal statute that sets locally prevailing wages and fringe benefits, through wage determinations, on service contracts over $2,500.
The schedule of prevailing wage and fringe rates, by locality and occupation, attached to a Service Contract Act contract as a floor.
The Service Contract Act fringe benefit rate per hour: $5.55 from July 2025, $5.09 where EO 13706 applies, and $2.42 or $1.96 in Hawaii.
A contract clause naming individuals essential to performance who cannot be diverted or replaced without the contracting officer's written consent.
Replacing a named key person under the contract's clause: written consent, notice and a substitute who meets or exceeds the requirement.
GAO's rule that an offeror who knows a proposed key person has become unavailable before award must tell the agency; the Court of Federal Claims reads the duty more narrowly.
GAO's protest standard for a proposal that knowingly or negligently relies on personnel the firm has no reasonable basis to furnish.
A contract characterized by an employer-employee relationship between the government and the contractor's staff; barred unless a statute authorizes it.
A FAR category of work the pack carries only by its location: the overhaul rulemaking moves it from subpart 7.5 to subpart 37.3.
FAR 52.219-14: on a set-aside services contract, no more than 50 percent of the amount paid may go to subcontractors that are not similarly situated.
FAR 52.244-2: without an approved purchasing system, the contracting officer's advance consent is needed before a cost-type, T&M or labor-hour subcontract.
An agreement between firms to pursue or perform work together; its hiring and pay terms fall under the DOJ/FTC worker guidelines.
An agreement between employers not to recruit, solicit or hire each other's workers; illegal under the 2025 DOJ/FTC guidelines and prosecutable as a felony.
A term barring solicitation of a firm's workers or customers; it survives antitrust review only as a collateral, necessary part of a real collaboration.
A covenant restricting a worker's later employment; a state-law question since the FTC acceded to the vacatur of its 2024 rule on September 5, 2025.
Pay during a post-employment restriction; the pack carries the term only as the consideration Massachusetts's noncompete statute may require.
A term requiring a worker to repay training costs on leaving; nearly 10 percent of workers were covered in 2020, and states now bar or narrow such terms.
A term that makes a worker pay or forfeit something for leaving before a date; limited by statute in four states, with New York and Washington to follow in 2027.
A promise to repay the employer if employment ends before a stated time; barred in Connecticut since 1985 and unenforceable in New York from February 13, 2027.
The tax exclusion for up to $5,250 a year of employer-paid education or student-loan payments under a separate written plan; indexed after 2026.
Training hours that count as hours worked for non-exempt employees unless all four FLSA conditions hold: outside hours, voluntary, not job related, no concurrent work.
Paid work with related instruction and mentoring under standards registered with DOL or a state agency; about 940,000 participants in FY2024.
The DoD program that places transitioning service members with an industry partner in their last 180 days, on military pay, under an MOU with offer obligations.
The federal law requiring employers of 100 or more to give 60 days' written notice before a plant closing or mass layoff affecting 50 or more at one site.
A state layoff-notice law with its own thresholds; fifteen states are reported to have one, most below the federal 100-employee line.
The federal default that a proper invoice is paid 30 days after receipt, with improper invoices returned within 7 days and interest paid automatically on late payment.
The FAR 32.009 policy that agencies pay small business contractors with a goal of 15 days after a proper invoice, and that primes pass it to small subcontractors.
A contract or order reserved for small business under a program status; on a services set-aside the prime keeps at least half the amount paid.
The firm holding the government contract and answering for its performance, with subcontractors and teammates working under it.
A firm that contracts with a prime to furnish supplies or services for performance of the prime contract.
The re-competition of a contract at the end of its term; a visible end date that the retain records treat as a withdrawal cognition.
The contractor that takes over a service contract after a recompete; it owes the Service Contract Act floors but no right of first refusal to the incumbent's staff.
The former federal rule giving service-contract employees a right of first refusal with a successor contractor; revoked in 2025 and rescinded December 22, 2025.
The federal electronic work-authorization check; FAR clause 52.222-54 requires it on contracts over $150,000 lasting 120 days or more with work in the United States.
The employment eligibility verification form every U.S. hire completes; Section 2 is due within three business days of the start, with the employee choosing the documents.
Under ITAR, releasing or transferring technical data to a foreign person in the United States is an export to every country of that person's citizenship or permanent residency.
The International Traffic in Arms Regulations at 22 CFR, whose deemed-export rule and U.S.-person definition shape hiring for controlled work.
The second export-control regime the hiring rules name beside ITAR, cited at 15 CFR parts 734 and 772; it contains no hiring requirement.
For export control, a lawful permanent resident or a protected individual under 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3): citizens, nationals, permanent residents, refugees and asylees.
The work visa for foreign professionals; a $100,000 entry payment was extended on September 21, 2026 but is uncollected under a court vacatur, and a $103,265 fee is proposed.
The Office of Federal Contract Compliance Programs, the DOL office whose 2026 rules rescinded the EO 11246 regulations and updated Section 503 and VEVRAA.
The contractor affirmative-action order revoked by EO 14173 in January 2025; its implementing regulations are removed effective October 26, 2026.
The Vietnam Era Veterans' Readjustment Assistance Act, whose clause requires a covered contractor to list every opening with the state workforce agency; threshold $200,000 from 2026.
The statutory contractor requirement that survives the EO 11246 rescission with a written plan at 50 employees and a $50,000 contract; its 7 percent goal is rescinded.
Title VII §703(g): refusing to hire or discharging someone for a position subject to a national-security requirement they do not meet is not unlawful.
The federal law governing employer use of third-party background reports: stand-alone disclosure, written permission and the two-notice adverse-action sequence.
A third-party background report on an applicant, governed by the FCRA's disclosure, permission and notice rules.
The FCRA notice sent after a decision against the person based on a consumer report, preceded by a pre-adverse-action notice with the report and the rights summary.
A state or local law requiring a pay range in the job posting itself; fourteen states and DC by October 2026, with Delaware in 2027.
A state or local law barring employers from asking applicants about prior pay; about twenty statewide bans, with Virginia added July 1, 2026.
The federal law requiring equal pay for substantially equal work in the same establishment, with four defenses and no cure by cutting anyone's pay.
The narrowing of pay differences between new hires and incumbents, or across peers, that a market-rate offer creates and the law forbids curing downward.
The FAR subpart 26.5 duty on larger contracts: a policy, an awareness program and conviction reporting, with no testing; the DFARS testing clause was reserved in May 2026.
A state law protecting off-duty cannabis use or barring pre-employment THC tests; nine adult-use states have one, and every one excepts federal contracts and clearance work.
A state law limiting employer credit checks; the vendor map lists thirteen states, DC and Puerto Rico, several excepting positions that require a security clearance.
The duty to keep application and selection records: one year from the record or the action under 29 CFR 1602.14, longer once a charge is filed, four years under California's ADS rules.
Eligibility for access to classified information, requested by a sponsoring contractor for an employee a classified contract needs and decided by the government.
The distinction the pack draws between a favorable eligibility determination and the separate decisions, by separate owners, that put the hire at a desk.
The entity eligibility determination a firm must hold before it can sponsor anyone; the firm cannot apply for it, a contracting activity or a cleared prime sponsors it.
The request a cleared contractor makes for an employee's eligibility, allowed only for access a classified contract needs; a candidate cannot start a clearance alone.
The National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual, now the rule at 32 CFR part 117, which fixes who a contractor can get cleared, when, and what it must report.
The Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency, whose industry investigations, vetting systems and timeliness figures set the clock a sponsored hire waits on.
The government's end-to-end personnel vetting system, with eApp as its electronic questionnaire; its roadmap runs to Trusted Workforce 2.0 full operating capability in FY2028 Q1.
The system in which a facility security officer sees investigations and personnel security determinations; DISS in the 2022 roadmap, DISS-JVS on the NBIS roadmap.
The electronic questionnaire within NBIS through which a sponsored hire submits the investigative form; the 2022 roadmap calls the questionnaire system e-QIP.
The questionnaire a sponsored hire submits, with fingerprints, to start the investigation; the pack's sources call it the questionnaire or the investigative standard form.
Interim eligibility granted before the final determination, only where no adverse information appears, for up to a year, not valid for RD, COMSEC or NATO information, and withdrawable without appeal.
The SEAD 7 rule that an agency accepts another authorized agency's investigation and adjudication, decided within five business days, unless one of seven exceptions applies.
Enrollment of cleared people in standing checks under Trusted Workforce 2.0: 78 percent of the covered population in FY2026 Q3, with full enrollment planned for September 2028.
The government-wide personnel-vetting reform whose quarterly report sets the 40- and 75-day timeliness targets and whose milestones run to full operating capability in FY2028 Q1.
The thirteen SEAD 4 guidelines, weighed under the whole-person concept, against which every eligibility decision is made; financial issues are the most common in appeals.
The statute that bars eligibility outright for an unlawful drug user or addict, with no waiver, and bars SCI, SAP and RD access after a year's incarceration or a dishonorable discharge.
A lie-detector examination the government may administer to defense and intelligence contractor staff; scheduled after a preliminary determination and never a ground for denying reciprocity.
Information to which access is a separate read-in beyond the clearance level: SCI access on a temporary basis is the granting authority's own decision, and a Bond Amendment disqualifier bars it.
The higher clearance level: an industry Top Secret took 243 days end to end in FY2026 Q3, paid an average $124,084 in the 2025 survey, and is never available to a non-U.S. citizen.
The clearance level whose industry cases took 197 days end to end in FY2026 Q3; average pay $100,296 in the 2025 survey, about $9,500 over Confidential.
DCSA's count of pending background investigations: about 121,000 in FY2026 Q3, up from about 101,000 the prior quarter.
Days from initiation to adjudication of a clearance case; DCSA's industry average was 197 days for a Secret and 243 for a Top Secret in FY2026 Q3, against targets of 40 and 75.
The DoD credential for facility and network access: sponsored by a DoD official, issued only after a favorable fingerprint check with an investigation submitted; an interim card does not transfer.
DoD Manual 8140.03: contracted staff in a cyberspace work role must hold the foundational qualification, by education, training or a listed certification, on the day the work starts.

The principle that access follows a demonstrated need; the pack carries it only as its rules state it: eligibility for access essential to a classified contract, and separate read-ins for SCI and SAP.
The National Industrial Security Program Policy Advisory Committee, at whose public meetings DCSA reports industry inventory and timeliness; its slides are the primary behind the clearance clock.
About 4.2 million clearance holders in October 2019, 1.35 million of them contractors or other, on the last public count; the pool is closed because no one can start a clearance alone.
The only route by which a non-U.S. citizen can be cleared, in rare cases and never for Top Secret, RD, COMSEC, intelligence or NATO information.
BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics: annual wage and employment estimates by occupation and metro area; May 2025 put software developers at a $148,100 mean.
The BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey: monthly openings, hires, quits and layoffs by industry; the pack's demand and churn indicators come from it.
The BLS quarterly index of wages and benefits: private-industry wages rose 3.1 percent and benefits 3.8 percent in the year to June 2026; the index behind the compensation cap.
The BLS quarterly measure of cost per hour worked for wages and each benefit; benefits were 30.0 percent of private-industry compensation in June 2026.
The JOLTS openings measure as a rate: 5.0 percent in professional and business services and 4.3 percent economy-wide in August 2026 (preliminary).
The JOLTS quits measure as a rate: 1.9 percent of total nonfarm employment, 3.1 million quits, in August 2026 (preliminary); the pack's churn indicator.
Days to the output the labor category assumes; output rose 53 percent over the first year where it could be counted, and no public benchmark exists for technical staff.
A current employer's raised offer to a departing employee; 58 percent of managers extend them and those who accept stay a mean 1.7 years, on a staffing firm's 2018 survey.
A one-time payment on hire; used by 80 percent of organizations and evaluated by 12 percent, and allowable on cost-type work only under a plan that predates the services.
A payment conditioned on staying; used by 66 percent of organizations, evaluated by 12 percent, and allowable on cost-type work only under an established plan.
An offer that states benefits and arrangements in dollars and terms a candidate can compare; benefits are 30 percent of compensation cost and arrangements are priced at 8 to 20 percent of pay.
External hires started about 18 percent above workers promoted into similar jobs at one financial-services firm, performed worse for two years and left more often.
The pay a worker gives up for an arrangement, or demands to accept one: about 8 percent of wages for a work-from-home option and about 20 percent to avoid short-notice schedules.
What workers say an arrangement is worth in pay: a mean 8 percent for two to three work-from-home days in the SWAA; 8 and 20 percent for home working and predictable schedules in the experiment.
The web of links, fit and sacrifice that makes leaving costly; corrected correlation −.26 with voluntary turnover across 29 studies, with on-the-job embeddedness the more predictive half.
Thoughts of quitting and intentions to leave; the strongest predictor of voluntary turnover, ρ .56 across 211 studies, with job search next at .40.
Turnover measured at the unit or firm level; across 82 studies it correlates about −.22 with customer satisfaction and production efficiency and −.15 with profit margin.
What replacing a departed employee costs as a share of salary: a 21 percent median across 27 case studies, 16 percent for jobs under $30,000 and up to 213 percent at the top.
The disputed figure for what a departure costs: practitioner multiples of 90 to 200 percent of salary name no study, against a measured case-study median near a fifth.
Firms promote on current performance even when other traits predict managerial success; a doubling of a manager's prior sales goes with 7.5 percent lower manager value added.
The organized ways a firm brings a newcomer in; institutionalized tactics correlate .24 to .40 with adjustment and the social ones, insiders as guides and investiture, .29 to .47.
The first ninety days, in which the hire learns the role, the tasks and the people; the onboard stage, whose evidence is the socialization meta-analyses and one firm's turnover study.
Role clarity, task mastery and social acceptance, the three things a newcomer has to acquire; they mediate the path from tactics to satisfaction, commitment, performance and staying.
An experienced insider beside the newcomer; the strongest onboarding tactic for the firm, with small measurable career gains for the protégé and a cost in senior billable hours.
Whether a trained skill is used on the job; supported by realistic practice, a supervisor who expects it (ρ .31), a transfer climate (.37) and an early chance to perform.
Skills any employer can use; theory says the worker should pay for them, the evidence says firms do, because the training firm knows the worker's ability better than the market.
Skill of use mainly to the current firm; firm-specific training is the practice most strongly tied to lower unit turnover, ρ −.40 across the unit-level studies.
A prime, customer or competitor hiring the person the firm trained and cleared; agreements not to do so are criminal, so the hold has to be in the job.
Hiring from employees' networks; referred workers quit 10 to 30 percent less across nine firms, and the networks are segregated, so the pool narrows as it improves.
What candidates believe the firm is as an employer; favorable images relate to better recruitment outcomes and form through recruiters and word of mouth.
Masculine-coded words in job ads, near-universal for male-dominated jobs, lower women's rated appeal and belonging for the same job without changing perceived skill requirements.
Replacing credential lines with skill requirements; announced at scale, it changed who was hired by less than one in 700 because the screens did not change.
A credential line in a posting; it shrinks the pool for little validity, since years of experience predicts performance at .07 and education was excluded for lack of data.
A person not actively searching for a job; the author's ledger row says strong candidates are not searching, and the evidence says such people are reached through networks and referrals.
Acquisition spend per hire as SHRM defines it; medians of $1,200 for nonexecutive and $10,625 for executive hires in 2025, with agency fees among the components.
The record of one opening to be filled; small organizations run a median of six per recruiter, and the plan stage asks whether each is funded, defined and priced before it is posted.
One accountable person who owns a requisition from opening to first productive day, with the calendar of every clock on it; the practice is unstudied.
Long-term strategies for acquiring, developing and retaining the workforce, in GAO's definition; the five principles are the reference shape for a firm's rolling forecast.
A dated list of expected openings by labor category, contract and probability, kept so the pipelines exist before the vacancies open; no study of forecast accuracy at small contractors was found.
What an open requisition costs: unbilled hours, delivery at risk, strain on the people covering it and the replacement cost, about a fifth of salary in the case-study median.
Carrying payroll before the funded work it was hired for begins; the payroll is indirect cost in the firm's rates, and a clearance cannot be requested ahead of a contract need.
Funded work identified for a sponsored hire while the clearance runs; contract hours are paid only for qualified labor on the contract, so other payroll is the firm's indirect cost.
Days from acceptance to the first productive day; each additional week raised the odds of a no-show by 22 percent among 157,154 accepted offers at one employer.
